elements.element: Customer may assign to an affiliate without consent.
elements.evidence: Second paragraph of 18.9 retained unchanged: "either Party shall have the right to assign this Agreement to an Affiliate, with the prior written consent of the other Party" — Affiliate assignment is consent-gated, and further blocked where the non-assigning Party reasonably believes material adverse tax consequences could result. No consent-free affiliate route for Customer was added.

elements.element: Customer may assign to a successor in a merger, acquisition, or sale of substantially all assets without consent.
elements.evidence: 18.9: "either Party may assign this Agreement without the other Party's consent to an entity that acquires substantially all of the business or assets of the assigning Party, whether by merger, acquisition or otherwise" — mutual, so it covers Customer.

elements.element: Vendor may not assign without Customer's consent.
elements.evidence: The same mutual successor carve-out lets Vendor (Array) assign to an acquirer of substantially all its business or assets without Customer's consent; the redline does not make the general consent requirement one-way against Vendor.

elements.element: Customer's consent to Vendor assignment is not to be unreasonably withheld.
elements.evidence: Inserted qualifier in 18.9 first sentence: "without the written consent of the other Party hereto (which shall not be unreasonably withheld or delayed)", which applies to Vendor-side requests for Customer consent.

elements.element: Vendor may never assign to a Customer competitor.
elements.evidence: No competitor bar appears anywhere in 18.9/18.10; 18.10 addresses only firewall procedures on a Change in Control of Array, not a prohibition on assignment to a Customer competitor.

elements.element: Customer's change of control gives Vendor no termination right.
elements.evidence: 18.10 imposes only firewall obligations on a Change in Control of Array (Vendor side); no operative provision in the cited text grants Vendor a termination or re-pricing right on a Customer (Ono) Change in Control, so the element's condition is satisfied by absence of any such right.

elements.element: Both parties may assign to a successor.
elements.evidence: 18.9: "except either Party may assign this Agreement without the other Party's consent to an entity that acquires substantially all of the business or assets of the assigning Party, whether by merger, acquisition or otherwise" — expressly mutual.

elements.element: A successor assignment requires written notice.
elements.evidence: 18.9 proviso: "the acquiring party agrees in a writing delivered to the non-assigning Party to assume all of the rights and obligations of the assigning Party" — a writing must be delivered to the non-assigning Party as a condition of the assignment, which supplies (and exceeds) written notice.

18.9 first sentence retains "This Agreement may not be assigned by either Party to any Third Party without the written consent of the other Party hereto", and the only other route — Affiliate assignment in the second paragraph — itself requires "the prior written consent of the other Party". No retained no-consent non-successor exception exists.

elements.element: Consent to other assignments is not to be unreasonably withheld.
elements.evidence: Redline adds "(which shall not be unreasonably withheld or delayed)" directly to the general consent requirement in 18.9, mirroring the standard already applied to Affiliate assignments in the same Section.

reasons: Fallback is position-complete: the mutual successor carve-out, the writing-delivered-to-the-non-assigning-Party condition, and the general written-consent requirement were already present, and the single inserted parenthetical supplies the missing reasonableness standard.

Preferred remains incomplete on three elements: affiliate assignment by Customer still requires prior written consent (and can be refused on a reasonable belief of adverse tax consequences), Vendor retains a consent-free successor assignment right, and there is no bar on Vendor assigning to a Customer competitor. To reach preferred the drafter would have to (i) carve Customer's Affiliate assignments out of the consent requirement, (ii) restrict the successor carve-out to Customer only, and (iii) add an express prohibition on Vendor assignment to a Customer competitor.

Minimality holds: the edit is a single in-line parenthetical in the first sentence of 18.9; no favourable existing language was deleted, no duplicate operative term was created, and no obligation outside the fallback checklist was added. The trailing "or delayed" is not a free-standing extra but a verbatim match to the consent standard already used in the second paragraph of the same Section, avoiding an internal inconsistency between two consent standards.

Intent preserved: the Affiliate route, the guarantee and assumption provisos, the tax-consequences carve-out, the competition-law clarification, the successors-and-permitted-assigns sentence, and Section 18.10's firewall mechanics all survive unchanged, with no dangling cross-reference or undefined term introduced.

The "deviation" classification is correct because the missing reasonableness standard is an express fallback atomic element, not merely a preferred-wording nicety; however, the residual gap is narrow and no walk-away trigger (blanket Customer assignment bar or Vendor change-of-control exit/re-pricing) is present.
